title: Reading Hebrews

objectives.can: Read the most literary Greek of the New Testament: balanced periods, rare vocabulary, μέν … δέ.

explanation.summary: Hebrews is often called the most carefully built Greek in the New Testament. Its sentences are long and balanced, its vocabulary is unusually varied, and it likes patterns such as μέν … δέ and a string of sentences that all begin with the same word. This lesson names those patterns, then sends you into the chapter on faith.

sections.heading: A period from the first words
body: The first four verses of Hebrews are a single sentence in which the main verb is held back. Hebrews 1:1 opens with two adverbs, Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως, which begin with the same sound (commentators usually note this as a sign of rhetorical polish), and then the subject ὁ θεὸς and a participle, λαλήσας: 'God, having spoken …'. The finite verb comes only in 1:2, ἐλάλησεν, from the same verb as the participle. Between the participle and the verb come the words 'long ago', 'to the fathers' and 'in the prophets'.

To read such a period, find the subject, then the participle that goes with it, and wait for the finite verb. Then see what is added after it. In 1:2 the relative clauses ὃν ἔθηκεν … δι’ οὗ καὶ ἐποίησεν carry the thought on to the Son, and 1:3 continues about him.

sections.heading: Relative, participles, and a late main verb
body: Hebrews 1:3 starts with a relative, ὃς ὢν …, 'who, being …', and follows it with more participles: φέρων, 'sustaining', and ποιησάμενος, 'having made'. The main verb, ἐκάθισεν, does not come until the end of a long run of phrases. This is the same skill as for 1 Peter: find the finite verb, then attach the participles.

Words are also chosen with care. In 1:3 ἀπαύγασμα and χαρακτήρ each occur only once in the analysed New Testament, and in 11:6 μισθαποδότης also occurs only once. Commentators regularly point to such rare or distinctive words as part of the author's style. The practical advice is simple: when a word is rare, look at its parts and at the context before reaching for a gloss.

sections.heading: μέν … δέ: balanced halves
body: μέν and δέ are a pair. μέν marks the first half of a balanced contrast, and δέ marks the second. μέν is often left untranslated in English; the contrast is carried by 'but' or 'while' in the second half. Hebrews uses the pair often.

In 1:7 the author writes πρὸς μὲν τοὺς ἀγγέλους λέγει, 'to the angels he says', and in 1:8 πρὸς δὲ τὸν υἱόν, 'but to the Son'. In the second half the verb λέγει is not repeated; it is understood from the first. Another example is 7:18–19, where ἀθέτησις μὲν γάρ is balanced by ἐπεισαγωγὴ δέ.

sections.heading: Repeated openings: the chapter on faith
body: Hebrews 11:1 begins with a plain statement: Ἔστιν δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων. ὑπόστασις and ἔλεγχος are two predicate nouns, each followed by a genitive participle, and both have a range of senses (translators differ on how to render them here), so it is better to watch how the sentence is built than to look for one gloss.

Clause after clause opens with the dative πίστει, 'by faith' or 'in faith': in 11:3, 11:4, 11:5, 11:7 and 11:8 (11:6 interrupts with a comment). A repeated opening like this is called anaphora, and it makes a list out of separate sentences. Each clause then says what a named person did or what happened. The dative πίστει is a dative of means or manner (a range of senses; read it from the sentence).

11:3 also shows the infinitive at work: νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας, a perfect passive infinitive after νοοῦμεν; and εἰς τὸ μὴ … γεγονέναι, an articular infinitive after εἰς. 11:5 has the perfect infinitive εὐαρεστηκέναι, and 11:6 the aorist εὐαρεστῆσαι from the same verb. The perfect infinitive often describes a completed state in relation to the main verb.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read Hebrews 11:1–8 once for the plan: a statement about faith, an appeal to the past, and then a list of people each introduced by πίστει. Read it again for the grammar, and for each verse ask three questions: what is the finite verb, what participle or infinitive hangs on it, and what does πίστει modify?

misunderstandings: Treating μέν as a word that must be translated. It prepares a contrast that δέ completes.
Looking for a verb in the second half of a μέν … δέ pair and finding none. The verb is often understood from the first half, as in 1:7–8.
Reading each πίστει in chapter 11 as the subject of the sentence. It is a dative and answers 'by what means' or 'in what way'.
Giving a rare word a single fixed gloss from one verse. The context and the word's parts decide.

deeper.heading: How the author writes
body: The author of Hebrews is unnamed, and scholars have long debated who wrote it. The Greek is the part of the question that can be examined directly: it uses periodic sentences, careful word order and rhetorical devices more than most of the New Testament. Whether that points to training in rhetoric is a matter of discussion; the grammar can show the patterns but not the person.

options: The Son, spoken of in the previous verse
check.explain: ὅς is masculine singular nominative, and it picks up the Son from ἐν υἱῷ … ὃν ἔθηκεν … δι’ οὗ in 1:2. The ages are accusative plural, and the angels are not mentioned until 1:4.

options: A genitive of comparison: better than the angels

options: There is no verb in either half

options: That person must believe that he exists
God must believe in that person

options: Aorist passive participles describing Noah: having been warned and having acted carefully, he built the ark
Main verbs of two separate sentences
check.explain: Both end in -θείς and agree with Νῶε. κατεσκεύασεν is the main verb, and the participles say in what circumstances he acted.

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: An articular infinitive after εἰς, with τὸ βλεπόμενον as its subject
A finite clause with the verb νοοῦμεν
check.explain: τό is the article of the infinitive γεγονέναι, a perfect infinitive, and τὸ βλεπόμενον is its accusative subject. Whether the construction gives purpose or result is a matter on which commentators differ.

reading.why: Eight verses that show the author's habits: a plain opening statement, anaphora with πίστει, infinitives of several tenses, participles ahead of the main verb, and rare words such as μισθαποδότης.
